entries.2acb5c5a58489bc5f76eb5cd02834957ebaf32aa: <div sID="gen9308" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Job.5" sID="Job.5"/> <div eID="gen9308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9309" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9310" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz, in the foregoing chapter, for the making good of his charge against Job, had vouched a word from heaven, sent him in a vision. In this chapter he appeals to those that bear record on earth, to the saints, the faithful witnesses of God's truth in all ages, <reference osisRef="Job.5.1">ver. 1</reference>. They will testify, I. That the sin of sinners is their ruin, <reference osisRef="Job.5.2-Job.5.5">ver. 2-5</reference>. II. That yet affliction is the common lot of mankind, <reference osisRef="Job.5.6-Job.5.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. III. That when we are in affliction it is our wisdom and duty to apply to God, for he is able and ready to help us, <reference osisRef="Job.5.8-Job.5.16">ver. 8-16</reference>. IV. That the afflictions which are borne well will end well; and Job particularly, if he would come to a better temper, might assure himself that God had great mercy in store for him, <reference osisRef="Job.5.17-Job.5.27">ver. 17-27</reference>. So that he concludes his discourse in somewhat a better humour than he began it.
entries.a6b65a31131f5995f7dbc87ea26e679d088a843a: <div eID="gen9310" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9309" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Address of Eliphaz. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9311" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Call now, if there be any that will answer thee; and to which of the saints wilt thou turn? <hi type="super">2</hi> For wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one. <hi type="super">3</hi> I have seen the foolish taking root: but suddenly I cursed his habitation. <hi type="super">4</hi> His children are far from safety, and they are crushed in the gate, neither <hi type="italic">is there</hi> any to deliver <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">5</hi> Whose harvest the hungry eateth up, and taketh it even out of the thorns, and the robber swalloweth up their substance. <div eID="gen9311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9312" type="x-p"/> A very warm dispute being begun between Job and his friends, Eliphaz here makes a fair motion to put the matter to a reference. In all debates perhaps the sooner this is done the better if the contenders cannot end it between themselves. So well assured is Eliphaz of the goodness of his own cause that he moves Job himself to choose the arbitrators (<reference osisRef="Job.5.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Call now, if there be any that will answer thee;</hi> that is, 1. "If there be any that suffer as thou sufferest. Canst thou produce an instance of any one that was really a saint that was reduced to such an extremity as thou art now reduced to? God never dealt with any that love his name as he deals with thee, and therefore surely thou art none of them." 2. "If there be any that say as thou sayest. Did ever any good man curse his day as thou dost? Or will any of the saints justify thee in these heats or passions, or say that these are the spots of God's children? Thou wilt find none of the saints that will be either thy advocates or my antagonists. <hi type="italic">To which of the saints wilt thou turn?</hi> Turn to which thou wilt, and thou wilt find they are all of my mind. I have the <hi type="italic">communis sensus fidelium—the unanimous vote of the faithful</hi> on my side; they will all subscribe to what I am going to say." Observe, (1.) Good people are called <hi type="italic">saints</hi> even in the Old Testament; and therefore I know not why we should, in common speaking (unless because we must <hi type="italic">loqui cum vulgo—speak as our neighbours</hi>), appropriate the title to those of the New Testament, and not say St. Abraham, St. Moses, and St. Isaiah, as well as St. Matthew and St. Mark; and St. David the psalmist, as well as St. David the British bishop. Aaron is expressly called <hi type="italic">the saint of the Lord.</hi> (2.) All that are themselves saints will turn to those that are so, will choose them for their friends and converse with them, will choose them for their judges and consult them. See <reference osisRef="Ps.119.79">Ps. cxix. 79</reference>. The saints shall <hi type="italic">judge the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.1-1Cor.6.2">1 Cor. vi. 1, 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Walk in the way of good men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.20">Prov. ii. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">the old way, the footsteps of the flock.</hi> Every one chooses some sort of people or other to whom he studies to recommend himself, and whose sentiments are to him the test of honour and dishonour. Now all true saints endeavour to recommend themselves to those that are such, and to stand right in their opinion. (3.) There are some truths so plain, and so universally known and believed, that one may venture to appeal to any of the saints concerning them. However there are some things about which they unhappily differ, there are many more, and more considerable, in which they are agreed; as the evil of sin, the vanity of the world, the worth of the soul, the necessity of a holy life, and the like. Though they do not all live up, as they should, to their belief of these truths, yet they are all ready to bear their testimony to them. <div eID="gen9312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9313" type="x-p"/> Now there are two things which Eliphaz here maintains, and in which he doubts not but all the saints concur with him:— <div eID="gen9313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9314" type="x-p"/> I. That the sin of sinners directly tends to their own ruin (<reference osisRef="Job.5.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wrath kills the foolish man,</hi> his own wrath, and therefore he is foolish for indulging it; it is a fire in his bones, in his blood, enough to put him into a fever. <hi type="italic">Envy</hi> is the rottenness of the bones, and so <hi type="italic">slays the silly one</hi> that frets himself with it. "So it is with thee," says Eliphaz, "while thou quarrellest with God thou doest thyself the greatest mischief; thy anger at thy own troubles, and thy envy at our prosperity, do but add to thy pain and misery: turn to the saints, and thou wilt find they understand their interest better." Job had told his wife she spoke as the foolish women; now Eliphaz tells him he acted as the foolish men, the silly ones. Or it may be meant thus: "If men are ruined and undone, it is always their own folly that ruins and undoes them. They kill themselves by some lust or other; therefore, no doubt, Job, thou hast done some foolish thing, by which thou hast brought thyself into this calamitous condition." Many understand it of God's wrath and jealousy. Job needed not be uneasy at the prosperity of the wicked, for the world's smiles can never shelter them from God's frowns; they are foolish and silly if they think they will. God's anger will be the death, the eternal death, of those on whom it fastens. What is hell but God's anger without mixture or period? <div eID="gen9314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9315" type="x-p"/> II. That their prosperity is short and their destruction certain, <reference osisRef="Job.5.3-Job.5.5">v. 3-5</reference>. He seems here to parallel Job's case with that which is commonly the case of wicked people. 1. Job had prospered for a time, seemed confirmed, and was secure in his prosperity; and it is common for foolish wicked men to do so: <hi type="italic">I have seen them taking root</hi>—planted, and, in their own and others' apprehension, fixed, and likely to continue. See <reference osisRef="Jer.12.2">Jer. xii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.35-Ps.37.36">Ps. xxxvii. 35, 36</reference>. We see worldly men taking root in the earth; on earthly things they fix the standing of their hopes, and from them they draw the sap of their comforts. The outward estate may be flourishing, but the soul cannot prosper that takes root in the earth. 2. Job's prosperity was now at an end, and so has the prosperity of other wicked people quickly been. (1.) Eliphaz foresaw their ruin with an eye of faith. Those who looked only at present things blessed their habitation, and thought them happy, blessed it long, and wished themselves in their condition. But Eliphaz cursed it, suddenly cursed it, as soon as he saw them begin to take root, that is, he plainly foresaw and foretold their ruin; not that he prayed for it (<hi type="italic">I have not desired the woeful day</hi>), but he prognosticated it. <hi type="italic">He went into the sanctuary,</hi> and there <hi type="italic">understood their end</hi> and heard their doom read (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.17-Ps.73.18">Ps. lxxiii. 17, 18</reference>), that the <hi type="italic">prosperity of fools will destroy them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.32">Prov. i. 32</reference>. Those who believe the word of God can see a <hi type="italic">curse in the house of the wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.33">Prov. iii. 33</reference>), though it be ever so finely and firmly built, and ever so full of all good things; and they can foresee that the curse will, in time, infallibly consume it with the timber thereof, and the stones thereof, <reference osisRef="Zech.5.4">Zech. v. 4</reference>. (2.) He saw, at length, what he had foreseen. He was not disappointed in his expectation concerning him; the event answered it; his family was undone, and his estate ruined. In these particulars he plainly and very invidiously reflects on Job's calamities. [1.] His children were crushed, <reference osisRef="Job.5.4">v. 4</reference>. They thought themselves safe in their eldest brother's house, but were <hi type="italic">far from safety,</hi> for they were <hi type="italic">crushed in the gate.</hi> Perhaps the door or gate of the house was highest built, and fell heaviest upon them, <hi type="italic">and there was none to deliver them</hi> from perishing in the ruins. This is commonly understood of the destruction of the families of wicked men, by the execution of justice upon them, to oblige them to restore what they have ill-gotten. They leave it to their children; but the descent shall not bar the entry of the rightful owners, who will crush their children, and cast them by due course of law (and there shall be none to help them), or perhaps by oppression, <reference osisRef="Ps.109.9-Ps.109.10">Ps. cix. 9</reference>, &c. [2.] His estate was plundered, <reference osisRef="Job.5.5">v. 5</reference>. Job's was so. The hungry robbers, the Sabeans and Chaldeans, ran away with it, and swallowed it; and this, says he, I have often observed in others. What has been got by spoil and rapine has been lost in the same way. The careful owner hedged it about with thorns, and then thought it safe; but the fence proved insignificant against the greediness of the spoilers (if hunger will break through the stone walls, much more through thorn hedges), and against the divine curse, which will go through the thorns and briers, and <hi type="italic">burn them together,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">Isa. xxvii. 4</reference>.
entries.360c215a83802dd75a81c9ce265bb0c954bf6f8c: <div eID="gen9315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9316" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Although affliction cometh not forth of the dust, neither doth trouble spring out of the ground; <hi type="super">7</hi> Yet man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward. <hi type="super">8</hi> I would seek unto God, and unto God would I commit my cause: <hi type="super">9</hi> Which doeth great things and unsearchable; marvellous things without number: <hi type="super">10</hi> Who giveth rain upon the earth, and sendeth waters upon the fields: <hi type="super">11</hi> To set up on high those that be low; that those which mourn may be exalted to safety. 12 He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform <hi type="italic">their</hi> enterprise. <hi type="super">13</hi> He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong. <hi type="super">14</hi> They meet with darkness in the daytime, and grope in the noonday as in the night. <hi type="super">15</hi> But he saveth the poor from the sword, from their mouth, and from the hand of the mighty. <hi type="super">16</hi> So the poor hath hope, and iniquity stoppeth her mouth. <div eID="gen9316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9317" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz, having touched Job in a very tender part, in mentioning both the loss of his estate and the death of his children as the just punishment of his sin, that he might not drive him to despair, here begins to encourage him, and puts him in a way to make himself easy. Now he very much changes his voice (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.20">Gal. iv. 20</reference>), and speaks in the accents of kindness, as if he would atone for the hard words he had given him. <div eID="gen9317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9318" type="x-p"/> I. He reminds him that no affliction comes by chance, nor is to be attributed to second causes: It <hi type="italic">doth not come forth of the dust,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">spring out of the ground,</hi> as the grass doth, <reference osisRef="Job.5.6">v. 6</reference>. It doth not come of course, at certain seasons of the year, as natural productions do, by a chain of second causes. The proportion between prosperity and adversity is not so exactly observed by Providence as that between day and night, summer and winter, but according to the will and counsel of God, when and as he thinks fit. Some read it, <hi type="italic">Sin comes not forth out of the dust, nor iniquity of the ground.</hi> If men be bad, they must not lay the blame upon the soil, the climate, or the stars, but on themselves. <hi type="italic">If thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it.</hi> We must not attribute our afflictions to fortune, for they are from God, nor our sins to fate, for they are from ourselves; so that, whatever trouble we are in, we must own that God sends it upon us and we procure it to ourselves: the former is a reason why we should be very patient, the latter why we should be very penitent, when we are afflicted. <div eID="gen9318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9319" type="x-p"/> II. He reminds him that trouble and affliction are what we have all reason to expect in this world: <hi type="italic">Man is brought to trouble</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.5.7">v. 7</reference>), not as man (had he kept his innocency he would have been born to pleasure), but as sinful man, as <hi type="italic">born of a woman</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.14.1">ch. xiv. 1</reference>), who was in the transgression. Man is born in sin, and therefore born to trouble. Even those that are born to honour and estate are yet born to trouble in the flesh. In our fallen state it has become natural to us to sin, and the natural consequence of that is affliction, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">Rom. v. 12</reference>. There is nothing in this world we are born to, and can truly call our own, but sin and trouble; both are as the sparks that fly upwards. Actual transgressions are the sparks that fly out of the furnace of original corruption; and, being called <hi type="italic">transgressors from the womb,</hi> no wonder that we <hi type="italic">deal very treacherously,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">Isa. xlviii. 8</reference>. Such too is the frailty of our bodies, and the vanity of all our enjoyments, that our troubles also thence arise as naturally <hi type="italic">as the sparks fly upwards</hi>—so many are they, so thick and so fast does one follow another. Why then should we be surprised at our afflictions as strange, or quarrel with them as hard, when they are but what we are born to? Man is born to <hi type="italic">labour</hi> (so it is in the margin), is sentenced to eat his bread in the sweat of his face, which should inure him to hardness, and make him bear his afflictions the better. <div eID="gen9319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9320" type="x-p"/> III. He directs him how to behave himself under his affliction (<reference osisRef="Job.5.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">I would seek unto God; surely I would:</hi> so it is in the original. Here is, 1. A tacit reproof to Job for not seeking to God, but quarrelling with him: "Job, if I had been in thy case, I would not have been so peevish and passionate as thou art. I would have acquiesced in the will of God." It is easy to say what we would do if we were in such a one's case; but when it comes to the trial, perhaps it will be found not so easy to do as we say. 2. Very good and seasonable advice to him, which Eliphaz transfers to himself in a figure: "For my part, the best way I should think I could take, if I were in thy condition, would be to apply to God." Note, We should give our friends no other counsel than what we would take ourselves if we were in their case, that we may be easy under our afflictions, may get good by them, and may see a good issue of them. (1.) We must by prayer fetch in mercy and grace from God, seek to him as a Father and friend, though he contend with us, as one who is alone able to support and succour us. His favour we must seek when we have lost all we have in the world; to him we must address ourselves as the fountain and Father of all good, all consolation. <hi type="italic">Is any afflicted? let him pray.</hi> It is heart's-ease, a salve for every sore. (2.) We must by patience refer ourselves and our cause to him: <hi type="italic">To God would I commit my cause;</hi> having spread it before him, I would leave it with him; having laid it at his feet, I would lodge it in his hand. "<hi type="italic">Here I am, let the Lord do with me as seemeth him good.</hi>" If our cause be indeed a good cause, we need not fear committing it to God, for he is both just and kind. Those that would seek so as to speed must refer themselves to God. <div eID="gen9320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9321" type="x-p"/> IV. He encourages him thus to seek to God, and commit his cause to him. It will not be in vain to do so, for he is one in whom we shall find effectual help. <div eID="gen9321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9322" type="x-p"/> 1. He recommends to his consideration God's almighty power and sovereign dominion. In general, he <hi type="italic">doeth great things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.5.9">v. 9</reference>), great indeed, for he can do any thing, he doth do every thing, and all according to the counsel of his own will—great indeed, for the operations of his power are, (1.) <hi type="italic">Unsearchable,</hi> and such as can never be fathomed, can never be found out <hi type="italic">from the beginning to the end,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Eccl. iii. 11</reference>. The works of nature are mysterious; the most curious searches come far short of full discoveries and the wisest philosophers have owned themselves at a loss. The designs of Providence are much more deep and unaccountable, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Rom. xi. 33</reference>. (2.) <hi type="italic">Numerous,</hi> and such as can never be reckoned up. He doeth great <hi type="italic">things without number;</hi> his power is never exhausted, nor will all his purposes ever be fulfilled till the end of time. (3.) They are <hi type="italic">marvellous,</hi> and such as never can be sufficiently admired; eternity itself will be short enough to be spent in the admiration of them. Now, by the consideration of this, Eliphaz intends, [1.] To convince Job of his fault and folly in quarrelling with God. We must not pretend to pass a judgment upon his works, for they are unsearchable and above our enquiries; nor must we strive with our Maker, for he will certainly be too hard for us, and is able to crush us in a moment. [2.] To encourage Job to seek unto God, and to refer his cause to him. What more encouraging than to see that he is one to whom power belongs? He can do great things and marvellous for our relief, when we are brought ever so low. <div eID="gen9322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9323" type="x-p"/> 2. He gives some instances of God's dominion and power. <div eID="gen9323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9324" type="x-p"/> (1.) God doeth great things in the kingdom of nature: <hi type="italic">He gives rain upon the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.5.10">v. 10</reference>), put here for all the gifts of common providence, all the <hi type="italic">fruitful seasons</hi> by which he <hi type="italic">filleth our hearts with food and gladness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.14.17">Acts xiv. 17</reference>. Observe, When he would show what great things God does he speaks of his giving rain, which, because it is a common thing, we are apt to look upon as a little thing, but, if we duly consider both how it is produced and what is produced by it, we shall see it to be a great work both of power and goodness. <div eID="gen9324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9325" type="x-p"/> (2.) He doeth great things in the affairs of the children of men, not only enriches the poor and comforts the needy, by the rain he sends (<reference osisRef="Job.5.10">v. 10</reference>), but, in order to the advancing of those that are low, he <hi type="italic">disappoints the devices of the crafty;</hi> for <reference osisRef="Job.5.11">v. 11</reference> is to be joined to <reference osisRef="Job.5.12">v. 12</reference>. Compare with <reference osisRef="Luke.1.51-Luke.1.53">Luke i. 51-53</reference>. He hath <hi type="italic">scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts,</hi> and so hath <hi type="italic">exalted those of low degree,</hi> and <hi type="italic">filled the heart with good things.</hi> See, <div eID="gen9325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9326" type="x-p"/> [1.] How he frustrates the counsels of the proud and politic, <reference osisRef="Job.5.12-Job.5.14">v. 12-14</reference>. There is a supreme power that manages and overrules men who think themselves free and absolute, and fulfils its own purposes in spite of their projects. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The froward, that walk contrary to God and the interests of his kingdom, are often very crafty; for they are the seed of the old serpent that was noted for his subtlety. They think themselves wise, but, at the end, will be fools. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The Froward enemies of God's kingdom have their devices, their enterprises, and their counsels, against it, and against the loyal faithful subjects of it. They are restless and unwearied in their designs, close in their consultations, high in their hopes, deep in their politics, and fast-linked in their confederacies, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.2">Ps. ii. 1, 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> God easily can, and (as far as is for his glory) certainly will, blast and defeat all the designs of his and his people's enemies. How were the plots of Ahithophel, Sanballat, and Haman baffled! How were the confederacies of Syria and Ephraim against Judah, of Gebal, and Ammon, and Amalek, against God's Israel, the kings of the earth and the princes against the Lord and against his anointed, broken! The hands that have been stretched out against God and his church have not performed their enterprise, nor have the weapons formed against Sion prospered. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> That which enemies have designed for the ruin of the church has often turned to their own ruin (<reference osisRef="Job.5.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">He takes the wise in their own craftiness,</hi> and <hi type="italic">snares them in the work of their own hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.7.15-Ps.7.16">Ps. vii. 15, 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.15-Ps.9.16">ix. 15, 16</reference>. This is quoted by the apostle (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.19">1 Cor. iii. 19</reference>) to show how the learned men of the heathen were befooled by their own vain philosophy. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> When God infatuates men they are perplexed, and at a loss, even in those things that seem most plain and easy (<reference osisRef="Job.5.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">They meet with darkness</hi> even <hi type="italic">in the day-time:</hi> nay (as in the margin), <hi type="italic">They run themselves into darkness</hi> by the violence and precipitation of their own counsels. See <reference osisRef="Job.12.20">ch. xii. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.12.24">24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.12.25">25</reference>. <div eID="gen9326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9327" type="x-p"/> [2.] How he favours the cause of the poor and humble, and espouses that. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He exalts the humble, <reference osisRef="Job.5.11">v. 11</reference>. Those whom proud men contrive to crush he raises from under their feet, and sets them in safety, <reference osisRef="Ps.12.5">Ps. xii. 5</reference>. The lowly in heart, and those that mourn, he advances, comforts, and makes to <hi type="italic">dwell on high,</hi> in the <hi type="italic">munitions of rocks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.33.16">Isa. xxxiii. 16</reference>. Sion's mourners are the sealed ones, marked for safety, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.4">Ezek. ix. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He delivers the oppressed, <reference osisRef="Job.5.15">v. 15</reference>. The designs of the crafty are to ruin the poor. Tongue, and hand, and sword, and all, are at work in order to this; but God takes under his special protection those who, being poor and unable to help themselves, being his poor and devoted to his praise, have committed themselves to him. He saves them from the mouth that speaks hard things against them and the hand that does hard things against them; for he can, when he pleases, tie the tongue and wither the hand. The effect of this is (<reference osisRef="Job.5.16">v. 16</reference>), 1. That weak and timorous saints are comforted: <hi type="italic">So the poor,</hi> who began to despair, <hi type="italic">has hope.</hi> The experiences of some are encouragement to others to hope the best in the worst of times; for it is the glory of God to send help to the helpless and hope to the hopeless. 2. That daring threatening sinners are confounded: <hi type="italic">Iniquity stops her mouth,</hi> being surprised at the strangeness of the deliverance, ashamed of its enmity against those who appear to be the favourites of Heaven, mortified at the disappointment, and compelled to acknowledge the justice of God's proceedings, having nothing to object against them. Those that domineered over God's poor, that frightened them, menaced them, and falsely accused them, will not have a word to say against them when God appears for them. See <reference osisRef="Ps.76.8-Ps.76.9">Ps. lxxvi. 8, 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa. xxvi. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.16">Mic. vii. 16</reference>.
entries.ffd929a2bc5a413491f5e35f204cd9d54ca02669: <div eID="gen9327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9328" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Behold, happy <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man whom God correcteth: therefore despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty: <hi type="super">18</hi> For he maketh sore, and bindeth up: he woundeth, and his hands make whole. <hi type="super">19</hi> He shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven there shall no evil touch thee. 20 In famine he shall redeem thee from death: and in war from the power of the sword. <hi type="super">21</hi> Thou shalt be hid from the scourge of the tongue: neither shalt thou be afraid of destruction when it cometh. <hi type="super">22</hi> At destruction and famine thou shalt laugh: neither shalt thou be afraid of the beasts of the earth. 23 For thou shalt be in league with the stones of the field: and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with thee. <hi type="super">24</hi> And thou shalt know that thy tabernacle <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> in peace; and thou shalt visit thy habitation, and shalt not sin. <hi type="super">25</hi> Thou shalt know also that thy seed <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> great, and thine offspring as the grass of the earth. <hi type="super">26</hi> Thou shalt come to <hi type="italic">thy</hi> grave in a full age, like as a shock of corn cometh in in his season. <hi type="super">27</hi> Lo this, we have searched it, so it <hi type="italic">is;</hi> hear it, and know thou <hi type="italic">it</hi> for thy good. <div eID="gen9328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9329" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz, in this concluding paragraph of his discourse, gives Job (what he himself knew not how to take) a comfortable prospect of the issue of his afflictions, if he did but recover his temper and accommodate himself to them. Observe, <div eID="gen9329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9330" type="x-p"/> I. The seasonable word of caution and exhortation that he gives him (<reference osisRef="Job.5.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty.</hi> Call it a chastening, which comes from the father's love and is designed for the child's good. Call it the chastening of the Almighty, with whom it is madness to contend, to whom it is wisdom and duty to submit, and who will be a God all-sufficient (for so the word signifies) to all those that trust in him. Do not <hi type="italic">despise</hi> it;" it is a copious word in the original. 1. "Be not averse to it. Let grace conquer the antipathy which nature has to suffering, and reconcile thyself to the will of God in it." We need the rod and we deserve it; and therefore we ought not to think it either strange or hard if we feel the smart of it. Let not the heart rise against a bitter pill or potion, when it is prescribed for our good. 2. "Do not think ill of it; do not put it from thee (as that which is either hurtful or at least not useful, which there is not occasion for nor advantage by) only because for the present it is not joyous, but grievous." We must never scorn to stoop to God, nor think it a thing below us to come under his discipline, but reckon, on the contrary, that God really magnifies man when he thus <hi type="italic">visits and tries him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.7.17-Job.7.18">ch. vii. 17, 18</reference>. 3. "Do not overlook and disregard it, as if it were only a chance, and the production of second causes, but take great notice of it as the voice of God and a messenger from heaven." More is implied than is expressed: "<hi type="italic">Reverence the chastening of the Lord;</hi> have a humble awful regard to this correcting hand, and tremble when the lion roars, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">Amos iii. 8</reference>. Submit to the chastening, and study to answer the call, to answer the end of it, and then you reverence it." When God by an affliction draws upon us for some of the effects he has entrusted us with we must honour his bill by accepting it, and subscribing it, resigning him his own when he calls for it. <div eID="gen9330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9331" type="x-p"/> II. The comfortable words of encouragement which he gives him thus to accommodate himself to his condition, and (as he himself had expressed it) to receive evil at the hand of God, and not despise it as a gift not worth the accepting. <div eID="gen9331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9332" type="x-p"/> 1. If his affliction was thus borne, (1.) The nature and property of it would be altered. Though it looked like a man's misery, it would really be his bliss: <hi type="italic">Happy is the man whom God correcteth</hi> if he make but a due improvement of the correction. A good man is happy though he be afflicted, for, whatever he has lost, he has not lost his enjoyment of God nor his title to heaven. Nay, he is happy because he is afflicted; correction is an evidence of his sonship and a means of his sanctification; it mortifies his corruptions, weans his heart from the world, draws him nearer to God, brings him to his Bible, brings him to his knees, works him for, and so is working for him, a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. <hi type="italic">Happy</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">is the man whom God correcteth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.1.12">Jam. i. 12</reference>. (2.) The issue and consequence of it would be very good, <reference osisRef="Job.5.18">v. 18</reference>. [1.] Though <hi type="italic">he makes sore</hi> the body with sore boils, the mind with sad thoughts, yet he <hi type="italic">binds up</hi> at the same time, as the skilful tender surgeon binds up the wounds he had occasion to make with his incision-knife. When God makes sores by the rebukes of his providence he binds up by the consolations of his Spirit, which oftentimes abound most as afflictions do abound, and counterbalance them, to the unspeakable satisfaction of the patient sufferers. [2.] Though <hi type="italic">he wounds,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">his hands make whole</hi> in due time; as he supports his people, and makes them easy under their afflictions, so in due time he delivers them, and makes a way for them to escape. All is well again; and he comforts them <hi type="italic">according to the time wherein he afflicted them.</hi> God's usual method is first to wound and then to heal, first to convince and then to comfort, first to humble and then to exalt; and (as Mr. Caryl observes) he never makes a wound too great, too deep, for his own cure. <hi type="italic">Una eademque manus vulnus opemque tulit—The hand that inflicts the wound applies the cure.</hi> God tears the wicked and goes away; let those heal that will, if they can (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">Hos. v. 14</reference>); but the humble and penitent may say, <hi type="italic">He has torn and he will heal us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1">Hos. vi. 1</reference>. This is general, but, <div eID="gen9332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9333" type="x-p"/> 2. In the <reference osisRef="Job.5.19-Job.5.27">following verses</reference> Eliphaz addresses himself directly to Job, and gives him many precious promises of great and kind things which God would do for him if he did but humble himself under his hand. Though then they had no Bibles that we know of, yet Eliphaz had sufficient warrant to give Job these assurances, from the general discoveries God had made of his good will to his people. And, though in every thing which Job's friends said they were not directed by the Spirit of God (for they spoke both of God and Job some things that were not right), yet the general doctrines they laid down expressed the pious sense of the patriarchal age, and as St. Paul quoted <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">v. 13</reference> for canonical scripture, and as the command <reference osisRef="Heb.12.5">v. 17</reference> is no doubt binding on us, so these promises here may be, and must be, received and applied as divine promises, and we may <hi type="italic">through patience and comfort of this</hi> part of <hi type="italic">scripture have hope.</hi> Let us therefore give diligence to make sure our interest in these promises, and then view the particulars of them and take the comfort of them. <div eID="gen9333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9334" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is here promised that as afflictions and troubles recur supports and deliverances shall be graciously repeated, be it ever so often: <hi type="italic">In six troubles he shall</hi> be ready to <hi type="italic">deliver thee; yea, and in seven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.5.19">v. 19</reference>. This intimates that, as long as we are here in this world, we must expect a succession of troubles, that the clouds will return after the rain. After six troubles may come a seventh; after many, look for more; but out of them all will God deliver those that are his, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.11">2 Tim. iii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">Ps. xxxiv. 19</reference>. Former deliverances are not, as among men, excuses from further deliverances, but earnests of them, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.19">Prov. xix. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen9334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9335" type="x-p"/> (2.) That, whatever troubles good men may be in, <hi type="italic">there shall no evil touch them;</hi> they shall do them no real harm; the malignity of them, the sting, shall be taken out; they may hiss, but they cannot hurt, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.10">Ps. xci. 10</reference>. The <hi type="italic">evil one toucheth not</hi> God's children, <reference osisRef="1John.5.18">1 John v. 18</reference>. Being kept from sin, they are kept from the evil of every trouble. <div eID="gen9335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9336" type="x-p"/> (3.) That, when desolating judgments are abroad, they shall be taken under special protection, <reference osisRef="Job.5.20">v. 20</reference>. Do many perish about them for want of the necessary supports of life? They shall be supplied. "<hi type="italic">In famine he shall redeem thee from death;</hi> whatever becomes of others, thou shalt be <hi type="italic">kept alive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.33.19">Ps. xxxiii. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Verily, thou shalt be fed,</hi> nay, even <hi type="italic">in the days of famine thou shalt be satisfied,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.3">Ps. xxxvii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.19">19</reference>. <hi type="italic">In</hi> time of <hi type="italic">war,</hi> when thousands fall on the right and left hand, he shall redeem thee <hi type="italic">from the power of the sword.</hi> If God please, it shall not touch thee; or if it wound thee, if it kill thee, it shall not hurt thee; it can but kill the body, nor has it power to do that unless it be given from above." <div eID="gen9336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9337" type="x-p"/> (4.) That, whatever is maliciously said against them, it shall not affect them to do them any hurt, <reference osisRef="Job.5.21">v. 21</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt</hi> not only be protected from the killing sword of war, but shalt <hi type="italic">be hidden from the scourge of the</hi> tongue, which, like a scourge, is vexing and painful, though not mortal." The best men, and the most inoffensive, cannot, even in their innocency, secure themselves from calumny, reproach, and false accusation. From these a man cannot hide himself, but God can hide him, so that the most malicious slanders shall be so little heeded by him as not to disturb his peace, and so little heeded by others as not to blemish his reputation: and the remainder of wrath God can and does restrain, for it is owing to the hold he has of the consciences of bad men that the scourge of the tongue is not the ruin of all the comforts of good men in this world. <div eID="gen9337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9338" type="x-p"/> (5.) That they shall have a holy security and serenity of mind, arising from their hope and confidence in God, even in the worst of times. When dangers are most threatening they shall be easy, believing themselves safe; and they <hi type="italic">shall not be afraid of destruction,</hi> no, not when they see it coming (<reference osisRef="Job.5.21">v. 21</reference>), nor <hi type="italic">of the beasts of the field</hi> when they set upon them, nor of men as cruel as beasts; nay, <hi type="italic">at destruction and famine thou shalt laugh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.5.22">v. 22</reference>), not so as to despise any of God's chastenings or make a jest of his judgments, but so as to triumph in God, in his power and goodness, and therein to triumph over the world and all its grievances, to be not only easy, but cheerful and joyful, in tribulation. Blessed Paul laughed at destruction when he said, <hi type="italic">O death! where is thy sting?</hi> when, in the name of all the saints, he defied all the calamities of this present time to <hi type="italic">separate us from the love of God,</hi> concluding that <hi type="italic">in all these things we are more than conquerors,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.35-Rom.8.39">Rom. viii. 35</reference>, &c. See <reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">Isa. xxxvii. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen9338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9339" type="x-p"/> (6.) That, being at peace with God, there shall be a covenant of friendship between them and the whole creation, <reference osisRef="Job.5.23">v. 23</reference>. "When thou walkest over thy grounds thou shalt not need to fear stumbling, for <hi type="italic">thou shalt be at league with the stones of the field,</hi> not to dash thy foot against any of them, nor shalt thou be in danger from <hi type="italic">the beasts of the field,</hi> for they shall all be at peace with thee;" compare <reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Hos. ii. 18</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field.</hi> This implies that while man is at enmity with his Maker the inferior creatures are at war with him; but <hi type="italic">tranquillus Deus tranquillat omnia—a reconciled God reconciles all things.</hi> Our covenant with God is a covenant with all the creatures that they shall do us no hurt but be ready to serve us and do us good. <div eID="gen9339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9340" type="x-p"/> (7.) That their houses and families shall be comfortable to them, <reference osisRef="Job.5.24">v. 24</reference>. Peace and piety in the family will make it so. "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt know</hi> and be assured <hi type="italic">that thy tabernacle</hi> is and <hi type="italic">shall be in peace;</hi> thou mayest be confident both of its present and its future prosperity." <hi type="italic">That peace is thy tabernacle</hi> (so the word is); peace is the house in which those dwell who dwell in God, and are at home in him. "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt visit</hi>" (that is, enquire into the affairs of) "<hi type="italic">thy habitation,</hi> and take a review of them, <hi type="italic">and shalt not sin.</hi>" [1.] God will provide a settlement for his people, mean perhaps and movable, a cottage, a tabernacle, but a fixed and quiet habitation. "Thou shalt not sin," or <hi type="italic">wander;</hi> that is, as some understand it, "thou shalt not be a fugitive and a vagabond" (Cain's curse), "but shalt dwell in the land, and verily, not uncertainly as vagrants, shalt thou be fed." [2.] Their families shall be taken under the special protection of the divine Providence, and shall prosper as far as is for their good. [3.] They shall be assured of peace, and of the continuance and entail of it. "Thou shalt know, to thy unspeakable satisfaction, that peace is sure to thee and thine, having the word of God for it." Providence may change, but the promise cannot. [4.] They shall have wisdom to govern their families aright, to order their affairs with discretion, and to look well to the ways of their household, which is here called <hi type="italic">visiting their habitation.</hi> Masters of families must not be strangers at home, but must have a watchful eye over what they have and what their servants do. [5.] They shall have grace to manage the concerns of their families after a godly sort, and not to sin in the management of them. They shall call their servants to account without passion, pride, covetousness, worldliness, or the like; they shall look into their affairs without discontent at what is or distrust of what shall be. Family piety crowns family peace and prosperity. The greatest blessing, both in our employments and in our enjoyments, is to be kept from sin in them. When we are abroad it is comfortable to hear that our tabernacle is in peace; and when we return home it is comfortable to visit our habitation with satisfaction in our success, that we have not failed in our business, and with a good conscience, that we have not offended God. <div eID="gen9340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9341" type="x-p"/> (8.) That their posterity shall be numerous and prosperous. Job had lost all his children; "but," says Eliphaz, "if thou return to God, he will again build up thy family, and thy seed shall be many and as great as ever, and thy offspring increasing and flourishing <hi type="italic">as the grass of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.5.25">v. 25</reference>), and thou shalt know it." God has blessings in store for the seed of the faithful, which they shall have if they do not stand in their own light and forfeit them by their folly. It is a comfort to parents to see the prosperity, especially the spiritual prosperity, of their children; if they are truly good, they are truly great, how small a figure soever they may make in the world. <div eID="gen9341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9342" type="x-p"/> (9.) That their death shall be seasonable, and they shall finish their course, at length, with joy and honour, <reference osisRef="Job.5.26">v. 26</reference>. It is a great mercy, [1.] To live to a full age, and not to have the number of our months cut off in the midst. If the providence of God do not give us long life, yet, if the grace of God give us to be satisfied with the time allotted us, we may be said to come to a full age. That man lives long enough that has done his work and is fit for another world. [2.] To be willing to die, to come cheerfully to the grave, and not to be forced thither, as he whose soul was required of him. [3.] To die seasonably, as the corn is cut and housed when it is fully ripe; not till then, but then not suffered to stand a day longer, lest it shed. Our times are in God's hand; it is well they are so, for he will take care that those who are his shall die in the best time: however their death may seem to us untimely, it will be found not unseasonable. <div eID="gen9342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9343" type="x-p"/> 3. In the <reference osisRef="Job.5.27">last verse</reference> he recommends these promises to Job, (1.) As faithful sayings, which he might be confident of the truth of: "<hi type="italic">Lo, this we have searched, and so it is.</hi> We have indeed received these things by tradition from our fathers, but we have not taken them upon trust; we have carefully searched them, have compared spiritual things with spiritual, have diligently studied them, and been confirmed in our belief of them from our own observation and experience; and we are all of a mind that so it is." Truth is a treasure that is well worth digging for, diving for; and then we shall know both how to value it ourselves and how to communicate it to others when we have taken pains in searching for it. (2.) As well worthy of all acceptation, which he might improve to his great advantage: <hi type="italic">Hear it, and know thou it for thy good.</hi> It is not enough to hear and know the truth, but we must improve it, and be made wiser and better by it, receive the impressions of it, and submit to the commanding power of it. <hi type="italic">Know it for thyself</hi> (so the word is), with application to thyself, and thy own case; not only "This is true," but "this is true concerning me." That which we thus hear and know for ourselves we hear and know for our good, as we are nourished by the meat which we digest. That is indeed a good sermon to us which does us good.  <chapter eID="Job.5"/> <div eID="gen9343" type="x-p"/>

entries.f417a172d5f0f9f7b73dbb91d9da009b63e2ef02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4529"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.5.1-Job.5.27">Job 5:1-27</reference>. Eliphaz' Conclusion from the Vision.</title> <div sID="gen6559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4529"/><hi type="bold">1. if there be any, &c.--</hi>Rather, "will He (God) reply to thee?" Job, after the revelation just given, cannot be so presumptuous as to think God or any of the holy ones (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.17">Da 4:17</reference>, "angels") round His throne, will vouchsafe a reply (a judicial expression) to his rebellious complaint. <div eID="gen6559" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d818024701c995039b9e275105029fc5bab51c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4530"/><div sID="gen6560" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4530"/><hi type="bold">2. wrath ... envy--</hi>fretful and passionate complaints, such as Eliphaz charged Job with (<reference osisRef="Job.4.5">Job 4:5</reference>; so <reference osisRef="Prov.14.30">Pr 14:30</reference>). Not, the wrath of God killeth the foolish, and His envy, &c. <div eID="gen6560" type="x-p"/>
entries.c55f2657b1adfa4840fbc1eb55bbf080b751f12f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4531"/><div sID="gen6561" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4531"/><hi type="bold">3. the foolish--</hi>the wicked. I have seen the sinner spread his "root" wide in prosperity, yet circumstances "suddenly" occurred which gave occasion for his once prosperous dwelling being "cursed" as desolate (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.35">Psa 37:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.36">36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">Jr 17:8</reference>). <div eID="gen6561" type="x-p"/>
entries.917909693fc0ea054f6184f01abc19c9f0119fd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4532"/><div sID="gen6562" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4532"/><hi type="bold">4. His children ... crushed in the gate--</hi>A judicial formula. The gate was the place of judgment and of other public proceedings (<reference osisRef="Ps.127.5">Psa 127:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.22">Pr 22:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.23.10">Ge 23:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.21.19">De 21:19</reference>). Such propylæa have been found in the Assyrian remains. Eliphaz obliquely alludes to the calamity which cut off Job's children. <div eID="gen6562" type="x-p"/>
entries.e019286a5d9c5b99070d8572c8d05c8a1bb7b4a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4533"/><div sID="gen6563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4533"/><hi type="bold">5. even out of the thorns--</hi>Even when part of the grain remains hanging on the thorn bushes (or, "is growing among thorns," <reference osisRef="Matt.13.7">Mt 13:7</reference>), the hungry gleaner does not grudge the trouble of even taking it away, so clean swept away is the harvest of the wicked.<div eID="gen6563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the robber--</hi>as the Sabeans, who robbed Job. Rather, translate "the thirsty," as the antithesis in the parallelism, "the hungry," proves. <div eID="gen6564" type="x-p"/>
entries.7426230259349e13f31cf73df3e50bce7acde6dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4534"/><div sID="gen6565" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4534"/><hi type="bold">6. Although--</hi>rather, "for truly" [Umbreit].<div eID="gen6565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">affliction cometh not forth of the dust--</hi>like a weed, of its own accord. Eliphaz hints that the cause of it lay with Job himself. <div eID="gen6566" type="x-p"/>
entries.80298301051bd9f6e762f6362f90ebbe55eda63d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4535"/><div sID="gen6567" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4535"/><hi type="bold">7. Yet--</hi>rather, "Truly," or, But affliction does not come from chance, but is the appointment of God for sin; that is, the original birth-sin of man. Eliphaz passes from the particular sin and consequent suffering of Job to the universal sin and suffering of mankind. Troubles spring from man's common sin by as necessary a law of natural consequences as sparks (Hebrew, "sons of coal") fly upward. Troubles are many and fiery, as sparks (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.12">1Pe 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.2">Is 43:2</reference>). Umbreit for "sparks" has "birds of prey;" literally, "sons of lightning," not so well. <div eID="gen6567" type="x-p"/>
entries.490b7d7d25547b9cac766a0aa674463bf2ae7def: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4536"/><div sID="gen6568" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4536"/>8. Therefore (as affliction is ordered by God, on account of sin), "I would" have you to "seek unto God" (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Is 8:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.8">Am 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.24">Jr 5:24</reference>). <div eID="gen6568" type="x-p"/>
entries.87b48817d03e7f2669d2ab1a1a2c4e08fe084585: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4537"/><div sID="gen6569" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4537"/>11. Connected with <reference osisRef="Job.5.9">Job 5:9</reference>. His "unsearchable" dealings are with a view to raise the humble and abase the proud (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.52">Lu 1:52</reference>). Therefore Job ought to turn humbly to Him. <div eID="gen6569" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ed1a7cc0ebd68e273b482602bda6b18b044f3da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4538"/><div sID="gen6570" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4538"/><hi type="bold">12. enterprise--</hi>literally, "realization." The Hebrew combines in the one word the two ideas, wisdom and happiness, "enduring existence" being the etymological and philosophical root of the combined notion [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6570" type="x-p"/>
entries.39fdf7c15e0286971fa2975d35d23e4d2c7f90c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4539"/><div sID="gen6571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4539"/>13. Paul (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.19">1Co 3:19</reference>) quoted this clause with the formula establishing its inspiration, "it is written." He cites the exact Hebrew words, not as he usually does the Septuagint, Greek version (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.15">Psa 9:15</reference>). Haman was hanged on the gallows he prepared for Mordecai (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.14">Es 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.7.10">7:10</reference>).<div eID="gen6571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the wise--</hi>that is, "the cunning."<div eID="gen6572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6573" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is carried headlong--</hi>Their scheme is precipitated before it is ripe. <div eID="gen6573" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1c8a2c765b7763537b081aded6639c0aac95d6c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4540"/><div sID="gen6574" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4540"/>14. Judicial blindness often is sent upon keen men of the world (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.29">De 28:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.10">Is 59:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.9.39">Joh 9:39</reference>). <div eID="gen6574" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e9dd11296aa93c070b304d852e963cb6d4557c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4541"/><div sID="gen6575" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4541"/>15. "From the sword" which proceedeth "from their mouth" (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.7">Psa 59:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">57:4</reference>). <div eID="gen6575" type="x-p"/>
entries.1adfdab1534df41f67f586c10aeb3fdeca9a6315: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4542"/><div sID="gen6576" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4542"/><hi type="bold">16. the poor hath hope--</hi>of the interposition of God.<div eID="gen6576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">iniquity stoppeth her mouth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.107.42">Psa 107:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">Mi 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.15">Is 52:15</reference>). Especially at the last day, through shame (Jude 15; <reference osisRef="Matt.22.12">Mt 22:12</reference>). The "mouth" was the offender (<reference osisRef="Job.5.15">Job 5:15</reference>), and the mouth shall then be stopped (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.8">Is 25:8</reference>) at the end. <div eID="gen6577" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d1fd7f5c640250e0e72ca08677278cafe774296: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4543"/><div sID="gen6578" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4543"/><hi type="bold">17. happy--</hi>not that the actual suffering is joyous; but the consideration of the righteousness of Him who sends it, and the end for which it is sent, make it a cause for thankfulness, not for complaints, such as Job had uttered (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.11">He 12:11</reference>). Eliphaz implies that the end in this case is to call back Job from the particular sin of which he takes for granted that Job is guilty. Paul seems to allude to this passage in <reference osisRef="Heb.12.5">He 12:5</reference>; so <reference osisRef="Jas.1.12">Jas 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.12">Pr 3:12</reference>. Eliphaz does not give due prominence to this truth, but rather to Job's sin. It is Elihu alone (Job 32:1-37:24) who fully dwells upon the truth, that affliction is mercy and justice in disguise, for the good of the sufferer. <div eID="gen6578" type="x-p"/>
entries.2579674f4c919cf166763f7ccc3b46b098c4eaf2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4544"/><div sID="gen6579" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4544"/><hi type="bold">18. he maketh sore, and bindeth up--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.39">De 32:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1">Ho 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.6">1Sa 2:6</reference>). An image from binding up a wound. The healing art consisted much at that time in external applications. <div eID="gen6579" type="x-p"/>
entries.3efd1df2fd2609f4d76fd13fb9312e2be02b38ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4545"/><div sID="gen6580" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4545"/><hi type="bold">19. in six ... yea, in seven--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.6.16">Pr 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.3">Am 1:3</reference>). The Hebrew idiom fixes on a certain number (here "six"), in order to call attention as to a thing of importance; then increases the force by adding, with a "yea, nay seven," the next higher number; here "seven," the sacred and perfect number. In all possible troubles; not merely in the precise number "seven." <div eID="gen6580" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca0b224bc3c9c15b5020bdfd5fb9a7b0563925c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4546"/><div sID="gen6581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4546"/><hi type="bold">20. power--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.5.12">Jr 5:12</reference>). Hebrew, "hands."<div eID="gen6581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the sword--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.35.5">Eze 35:5</reference>, Margin). Hands are given to the sword personified as a living agent. <div eID="gen6582" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f4de5c371fb08b6d2e1f17726c1618099125838: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4547"/><div sID="gen6583" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4547"/>21. (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">Psa 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">Jr 18:18</reference>). Smite (Psalm 73. 9). <div eID="gen6583" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5e1c59816bea804c4a3cfaf2b5a43b51852a156: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4548"/><div sID="gen6584" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4548"/><hi type="bold">22. famine thou shalt laugh--</hi>Not, in spite of destruction and famine, which is true (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.17">Ha 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.18">18</reference>), though not the truth meant by Eliphaz, but because those calamities shall not come upon thee. A different Hebrew word from that in <reference osisRef="Job.5.20">Job 5:20</reference>; there, famine in general; here, the languid state of those wanting proper nutriment [Barnes]. <div eID="gen6584" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a041d083ba8dcb61efc1f1a78dc9b65df1e939a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4549"/><div sID="gen6585" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4549"/><hi type="bold">23. in league with the stones of the field--</hi>They shall not hurt the fertility of thy soil; nor the wild beasts thy fruits; spoken in Arabia-Deserta, where stones abounded. Arabia, derived from Arabah--a desert plain. The first clause of this verse answers to the first clause of <reference osisRef="Job.5.22">Job 5:22</reference>; and the last of this verse to the last of that verse. The full realization of this is yet future (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.23">Is 65:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Ho 2:18</reference>). <div eID="gen6585" type="x-p"/>
entries.67877a193b9fb99cf1303c32c8cad9341552055d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4550"/><div sID="gen6586" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4550"/><hi type="bold">24. know--</hi>"Thou shalt rest in the assurance, that thine habitation is the abode of peace; and (if) thou numberest thine herd, thine expectations prove not fallacious" [Umbreit]. "Sin" does not agree with the context. The Hebrew word--"to miss" a mark, said of archers (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.16">Jud 20:16</reference>). The Hebrew for "habitation" primarily means "the fold for cattle"; and for "visit," often to "take an account of, to number." "Peace" is the common Eastern salutation; including inward and outward prosperity. <div eID="gen6586" type="x-p"/>
entries.d058abbc6e3ebec11bf9cdaf649f28788c4d26fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4551"/><div sID="gen6587" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4551"/><hi type="bold">25. as the grass--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.72.16">Psa 72:16</reference>). Properly, "herb-bearing seed" (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.11">Ge 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen6587" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca40cf4a963f179bb27493bf93f16bcb082904df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4552"/><div sID="gen6588" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4552"/><hi type="bold">26. in a full age--</hi>So "full of days" (<reference osisRef="Job.42.17">Job 42:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.29">Ge 35:29</reference>). Not mere length of years, but ripeness for death, one's inward and outward full development not being prematurely cut short, is denoted (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.22">Is 65:22</reference>).<div eID="gen6588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou shalt come--</hi>not literally, but expressing willingness to die. Eliphaz speaks from the Old Testament point of view, which made full years a reward of the righteous (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.16">Psa 91:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.20.12">Ex 20:12</reference>), and premature death the lot of the wicked (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.23">Psa 55:23</reference>). The righteous are immortal till their work is done. To keep them longer would be to render them less fit to die. God takes them at their best (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Is 57:1</reference>). The good are compared to wheat (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.30">Mt 13:30</reference>).<div eID="gen6589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cometh in--</hi>literally, "ascends." The corn is lifted up off the earth and carried home; so the good man "is raised into the heap of sheaves" [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6590" type="x-p"/>
entries.64db3e0470938e446b12caca48c1bb9b51cfed94: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4553"/><div sID="gen6591" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4553"/><hi type="bold">27. searched it ... for thy good--</hi>literally, "for thyself" (<reference osisRef="Ps.111.2">Psa 111:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.2.4">Pr 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.12">9:12</reference>). <chapter eID="Job.5"/>

entries.72d13c13a17933ef630fa81450617e1730dcf7a9: <div eID="gen16021" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16022" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16023" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16023" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16022" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16024" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz proceeds to show that the wicked are always punished by the justice of God, though they may appear to flourish for a time, <reference osisRef="Job.5.1-Job.5.8">Job 5:1-8</reference>; extols the providence of God, by which the counsels of the wicked are brought to naught, and the poor fed and supported, <reference osisRef="Job.5.9-Job.5.16">Job 5:9-16</reference>; shows the blessedness of being corrected by God, in the excellent fruits that result from it; and exhorts Job to patience and submission, with the promise of all secular prosperity, and a happy death in a mature and comfortable old age, <reference osisRef="Job.5.17-Job.5.27">Job 5:17-27</reference>. <div eID="gen16024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16025" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen16025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16026" type="x-p"/> Call now, if there be any - This appears to be a strong irony. From whom among those whose foundations are in the dust, and who are crushed before the moth, canst thou expect succor? <div eID="gen16026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16027" type="x-p"/> To which of the saints wilt thou turn? - To whom among the holy ones, (קדשים kedoshim), or among those who are equally dependent on Divine support with thyself, and can do no good but as influenced and directed by God, canst thou turn for help? Neither angel nor saint can help any man unless sent especially from God; and all prayers to them must be foolish and absurd, not to say impious. Can the channel afford me water, if the fountain cease to emit it?
entries.50d4be6e44335846410f7469b0b227239f12dd23: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16028" type="x-p"/> For wrath killeth the foolish man - Foolish, silly, and simple, are epithets given by Solomon to sinners and transgressors of all kinds. Such parallelisms have afforded a presumptive argument that Solomon was the author of this book. See the preface. The words of Eliphaz may be considered as a sort of maxim, which the wisdom and experience of ages had served to establish; viz., The wrath of God is manifested only against the wicked and impious; and if thou wert not such, God would not thus contend with thee.
entries.b1d940f375b5d27dce59155cd619f35b9d834803: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16029" type="x-p"/> I have seen the foolish taking root - I have seen wicked men for a time in prosperity, and becoming established in the earth; but I well knew, from God's manner of dealing with men, that they must soon be blasted. I even ventured to pronounce their doom; for I knew that, in the order of God's providence, that was inevitable. I cursed his habitation.
entries.9176c0cf9a28e8a8819fd201fe9f450955b8e5e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16030" type="x-p"/> His children are far from safety - His posterity shall not continue in prosperity. Ill gotten, ill spent; whatever is got by wrong must have God's curse on it. <div eID="gen16030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16031" type="x-p"/> They are crushed in the gate - The Targum says, They shall be bruised in the gate of hell, in the day of the great judgment. There is reference here to a custom which I have often had occasion to notice: viz., that in the Eastern countries the court-house, or tribunal of justice, was at the Gate of the city; here the magistrates attended, and hither the plaintiff and defendant came for justice.
entries.e75167566a8f4ad45b51fd5414045a0e6361d611: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16032" type="x-p"/> Whose harvest - Their possessions, because acquired by unjust means, shall not be under the protection of God's providence; he shall abandon them to be pillaged and destroyed by the wandering half-starved hordes of the desert banditti. They shall carry it suddenly off; even the thorns - grain, weeds, thistles, and all, shall they carry off in their rapacious hurry. <div eID="gen16032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16033" type="x-p"/> The robber swalloweth us - Or, more properly, the thirsty, צמים tsammim, as is plain from their swallowing up or gulping down; opposed to the hungry or half-starved, mentioned in the preceding clause. The hungry shall eat up their grain, and the thirsty shall drink down their wine and oil, here termed חילם cheylam, their strength or power, for the most obvious reasons. <div eID="gen16033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16034" type="x-p"/> There seem to be two allusions in this verse: 1. To the hordes of wandering predatory banditti, or half-starved Arabs of the desert, who have their scanty maintenance by the plunder of others. These descendants of Ishmael have ever had their hands against all men, and live to this day in the same predatory manner in which they have lived for several thousands of years. M. Volney's account of them is striking: "These men are smaller, leaner, and blacker, than any of the Bedouins yet discovered. Their wasted legs had only tendons without calves. Their belly was shrunk to their back. They are in general small, lean, and swarthy, and more so in the bosom of the desert than on the borders of the more cultivated country. They are ordinarily about five feet or five feet two inches high; they seldom have more than about six ounces of food for the whole day. Six or seven dates, soaked in melted butter, a little milk, or curd, serve a man for twenty-four hours; and he seems happy when he can add a small portion of coarse flour, or a little ball of rice. Their camels also, which are their only support, are remarkably meagre, living on the meanest and most scanty provision. Nature has given it a small head without ears, at the end of a long neck without flesh. She has taken from its legs and thighs every muscle not immediately requisite for motion; and in short has bestowed on its withered body only the vessels and tendons necessary to connect its frame together. She has furnished it with a strong jaw, that it may grind the hardest aliments; and, lest it should consume too much, she has straitened its stomach, and obliged it to chew the cud." Such is the description given of the Bedouin and his camel, by M. Volney, who, while he denies the true God, finds out a deity which he calls Nature, whose works evince the highest providence, wisdom, and design! And where does this most wonderful and intelligent goddess dwell? Nowhere but in the creed of the infidel; while the genuine believer knows that nature is only the agent created and employed by the great and wise God to accomplish, under his direction, the greatest and most stupendous beneficial effects. The second allusion in the verse I suppose to be to the loss Job had sustained of his cattle by the predatory Sabeans; and all this Eliphaz introduces for the support of his grand argument, to convict Job of hidden crimes, on which account his enemies were permitted to destroy his property; that property, because of this wickedness, being placed out of the protection of God's providence.
entries.d1e47e8ec660d27c550409d0e1a7e3eccc928d2b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16035" type="x-p"/> Affliction cometh not forth of the dust - If there were not an adequate cause, thou couldst not be so grievously afflicted. <div eID="gen16035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16036" type="x-p"/> Spring out of the ground - It is not from mere natural causes that affliction and trouble come; God's justice inflicts them upon offending man.
entries.58d56ec3f6a6a583e5c318cec0cb17432199b843: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16037" type="x-p"/> Yet man is born unto trouble - לעמל leamal, to labor. He must toil and be careful; and if in the course of his labor he meet with trials and difficulties, he should rise superior to them, and not sink as thou dost. <div eID="gen16037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16038" type="x-p"/> As the sparks By upward - ובני רשף יגביהי עוף ubeney resheph yagbihu uph; And the sons of the coal lift up their flight, or dart upwards. And who are the sons of the coal? Are they not bold, intrepid, ardent, fearless men, who rise superior to all their trials; combat what are termed chance and occurrence; succumb under no difficulties; and rise superior to time, tide, fate, and fortune? I prefer this to all the various meanings of the place with which I have met. Coverdale translates, It is man that is borne unto mysery, like as the byrde for to fle. Most of the ancient versions give a similar sense.
entries.c8235259fcf1189b03abc732e50e653c0f1102e5: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16039" type="x-p"/> I would seek unto God - Were I in your place, instead of wasting my time, and irritating my soul with useless complaints, I would apply to my Maker, and, if conscious of my innocence, would confidently commit my cause to him.
entries.503323c1632833ff549cea8d551dd71de01c24b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16040" type="x-p"/> Which doeth great things - No work, however complicated, is too deep for his counsel to plan; none, however stupendous, is too great for his power to execute. He who is upright is always safe in referring his cause to God, and trusting in him.
entries.a239b36adaae70567cef31bacc9e22d412872251: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16041" type="x-p"/> Who giveth rain upon the earth - The Chaldee gives this verse a fine turn: "Who gives rain on the face of the land of Israel, and sends waters on the face of the provinces of the people." Similar to our Lord's saying, which is expressed in the half of the compass: Your Father which is in heaven - Sendeth Rain on the Just and on the Unjust; <reference osisRef="Mat.5.45">Mat 5:45</reference>. <div eID="gen16041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16042" type="x-p"/> Sendeth waters upon the fields - The term חצות chutsoth, which we translate fields, and generally signifies streets, may here mean those plantations which are laid out in ridges or plats, in an orderly, regular manner. God does not only send rain upon the earth in a general manner, but, by an especial providence, waters the cultivated ground, so that not one ridge is destitute of its due proportion of fructifying moisture.
entries.af4279181454de3d8e8d14a60426ff72888b7def: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16043" type="x-p"/> To set up on high those that be low - He so distributes his providential blessings without partiality, that the land of the poor man is as well sunned and watered as that of the rich; so that he is thus set upon a level with the lords of the soil.
entries.ba1b3294704c5baf0582ccc4b49e55cbeb1e01c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16044" type="x-p"/> He disappointeth the devices of the crafty - All these sayings refer to God's particular providence, by which he is ever working for the good, and counterworking the plots of the wicked. And as various as are the contingent, capricious, and malevolent acts of men, so varied are his providential interferences; disappointing the devices, snares, and plots of the crafty, so that their plans being confounded, and their machinery broken in pieces, their hands cannot perform their enterprises.
entries.35937f8042beb063beb53440b34ff6a609bfde87: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16045" type="x-p"/> He taketh the wise in their own craftiness - So counterworks them as to cause their feet to be taken in their own snares, and their evil dealings to fall on their own pate. Such frequent proofs has God given of his especial interference in behalf of the innocent, who have been the objects of the plots and evil designs of the wicked, by turning those evil devices against their framers, that he who digs a pit for his neighbor shall fall into it himself has become a universal adage, and has passed, either in so many words or in sense, into all the languages of all the people of the earth. Lucretius expresses it strongly: <div eID="gen16045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16046" type="x-p"/> Circumretit enim vis atque injuria quemque, <div eID="gen16046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16047" type="x-p"/> Atque, unde exorta est, ad eum plerumque revortit. <div eID="gen16047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16048" type="x-p"/> Lucret. lib. v., ver. 1151. "For force and wrong entangle the man that uses them; <div eID="gen16048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16049" type="x-p"/> And, for the most part, recoil on the head of the contriver."
entries.11d59bb5e21235fcdf262910849bde16a7daebbf: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16050" type="x-p"/> They meet with darkness in the daytime - God confounds them and their measures; and, with all their cunning and dexterity, they are outwitted, and often act on their own projects, planned with care and skill, as if they had been the crudest conceptions of the most disordered minds. They act in noonday as if the sun were extinct, and their eyes put out. Thus does God "abate their pride, assuage their malice, and confound their devices."
entries.bda01b0e2e3469155adadc1f2bc4b775dac93f32: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16051" type="x-p"/> He saveth the poor from the sword, from their mouth - This is rather a harsh construction. To avoid this, some have proposed to render מחרב mechereb, which we translate from the sword, the persecuted, but, I am afraid, on very slender authority. Instead of מחרב מפיהם mechereb mippihem, "from the sword, from their mouth," eleven of Kennicott and De Rossi's MSS. read מחרב פיהם mechereb pihem, from the sword of their mouth; and with these MSS. the Chaldee, Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic agree. The verse, therefore, may be translated thus: - <div eID="gen16051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16052" type="x-p"/> He saveth from the sword of their mouth; <div eID="gen16052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16053" type="x-p"/> The poor from the hand of the mighty. <div eID="gen16053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16054" type="x-p"/> Or thus: - <div eID="gen16054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16055" type="x-p"/> He saveth from the sword of their mouth; <div eID="gen16055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16056" type="x-p"/> And with a strong hand the impoverished.
entries.707f5ffc725e3fadd926d02a1947ed53aaaf0553: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16057" type="x-p"/> So the poor - דל dal, he who is made thin, who is wasted, extenuated; hath hope - he sees what God is accustomed to do, and he expects a repetition of gracious dealings in his own behalf; and because God deals thus with those who trust in him, therefore the mouth of impiety is stopped. Religion is kept alive in the earth, because of God's signal interventions in behalf of the bodies and souls of his followers.
entries.8c4a31ba3dd1c106b779dac5f292aeaceda41a4e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16058" type="x-p"/> Behold, happy is the man - הנח hinneh, behold, is wanting in five of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., and also in the Syriac, Vulgate, and Arabic.
